strengths: The idea seems to be completely original, with multiple novel components and procedures.
The proposed structural adaptation method is interesting and novel.
The resulted networks show less model complexity compared to neural networks.
DIRAD is further applied in CL as an architecture based method to address forgetting.
weaknesses: The proposed method is completely new and extremely complex, and Section 3 and 4 are incapable of explaining the methodology properly.
Many terminologies are coined, yet the relevance of coining these terminologies is ill‑justified.
The complexity of the method requires many design choices, yet these choices seem to be determined arbitrarily (see P16L819 "Among the many ways to realize this condition, we choose ...").
The full Appendix still fails to capture the essence of the proposed method.
The paper is poorly written, with pieces of information scattered throughout.
Terminologies are not clearly defined before usage.
Run‑on sentences make the arguments hard to parse (e.g., P15L772 "Our goal with this point of modulation ...").

It is unclear whether designing such a complex framework is necessary, given that a familiarity autoencoder plugged into an adaptive network might achieve similar goals, and the proposed method yields marginal gains that do not scale to normal‑sized models and datasets.
The terminology "statistical conflict" is not formally defined despite being a key motivation for DIRAD.
The paper does not explain why the familiarity autoencoder cannot be simply plugged into any adaptive network for continual learning.
The related works section mentions many self‑expandable/adaptive network papers, yet none are included as baselines for comparison.
The paper fails to contextualize the proposed technique within the broader landscape of existing adaptive networks.
It is unclear how the proposed technique generalizes its performance to hold‑out datasets.
The greedy approach of ENC is prone to getting stuck in local minima or overfitting to noise, as the model expands capacity whenever the edge saturation condition triggers.

The major weakness lies in the scalability of the proposed method; the computational complexity increases a lot with high‑dimensional data, and in continual learning the edge generation process becomes prohibitively expensive as the number of nodes and input dimensionality increase, raising doubts about practical use and the significance of improvement.

The scale of experiments is limited by computational complexity, and more experimental results on larger datasets such as CIFAR and with more advanced baselines are needed to demonstrate the method's effectiveness on complex, real‑world data.
The paper should compare the proposed node validation technique with simpler out‑of‑distribution detection strategies and clarify how it performs when data distribution shifts are subtle or gradual.

The writing needs improvement; sections 3 and 4 are hard to follow, definitions of activation potentials (APs) and the conditions for edge generation are unclear, making it difficult to reproduce results or understand the underlying mechanisms.
The paper is hard to follow and uses technical terms and math notations without first defining them, and uses confusing terminology without properly setting the stage.
The figures are vague and small, and captions are inadequate to describe the experiments.
The paper only considers average accuracy, which is a poor indicator of performance in continual learning; it fails to report task‑wise accuracy, forward and backward transfer, and memory overhead.
The paper chooses EWC as a baseline, which is an outdated method that requires task IDs, making the comparison questionable.
The proposed approach does not address catastrophic forgetting; accuracy degrades over tasks, indicating possible forgetting of older tasks.
The experiments are limited to only three grayscale tasks (MNIST, F‑MNIST) which are low complexity; results may not generalize to more complex RGB datasets such as CIFAR‑10/100, ImageNet, FOOD‑1K.
The paper lacks theoretical proof that the CL method can retain performance on large task sets and relies heavily on empirical validation without testing on many tasks.
The literature review is insufficient; the paper does not compare with other constant‑capacity or capacity‑growing methods, nor with various replay strategies.
The writing is poor; the flow is abrupt, lacking pre‑context, making the paper hard to follow.
The paper lacks ablation studies to isolate contributions of different algorithmic modifications.
The paper lacks adversarial experiments to test robustness under complex or adversarial tasks.
